opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to accept that you can't anticipate it. I've spent my whole life trying to bet on the future, and the most important thing I learned is that no matter how much I know, what I don't know is much greater. So the real skill isn't knowing what's going to happen. It's knowing how to deal with not knowing.

In the markets, that means diversifying, so you're not dependent on any one outcome. The same applies to a career. Don't build yourself around one narrow skill or one prediction about which industry is going to win, because the world is changing too fast, especially with AI. A lot of what people learn in school today is going to be done by machines.

So what do you develop? First, learn how to learn. Be curious, and be able to pick up new things throughout your life, because you'll have to. Second, know yourself. Everybody's wired differently. Some people are big-picture thinkers, others are great with details. Understand your strengths and your weaknesses, and then find people who are strong where you're weak. That's been one of the biggest keys for me. Third, learn how to think independently and stress-test your thinking with smart people who disagree with you. Being radically open-minded is an enormous advantage, because pain plus reflection equals progress. You're going to make mistakes, so treat each one as a puzzle, and when you solve it, you get a gem, a principle you can use next time.

And don't underestimate the human part: having meaningful relationships and being someone people can trust. Those things carry you through whatever comes.

The other practical thing is financial. Save enough to have a cushion, ideally something like six months of living expenses, and eventually more, because savings give you options and freedom. That way, when the world changes, you can adapt rather than be crushed by it.

So I'd say don't try to predict the future. Prepare so that you'll do well across the range of futures that could happen. Then go after what you're passionate about, because if you love what you do and you keep learning and evolving, you'll be okay.

r001.rationale: It recommends learning how to learn and continuing to acquire new skills throughout life as the future changes.

r002.rationale: It advises against relying on one narrow skill or an industry prediction, but does not clearly warn that presenting a particular occupation as the answer would be misleading.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you're right that you can't anticipate the future, and the people who get in trouble are the ones who think they can. So the question isn't really "what will the future be?" It's "how do I become the kind of person who does well no matter what the future is?"

And I think that comes down to a few things.

The first is knowing yourself. Most young people spend all their time looking outward at what's hot, what pays, what their parents or their friends think is impressive. They don't look inward. But you have a nature. You're wired a certain way. Some people are creative and chaotic, some people are precise and orderly, some people love being with others, some people need to be alone. If you pick a path that fights your nature, you'll be miserable and you'll be mediocre, because you're competing against people who are built for that thing. So step one is: figure out what you're like, figure out what you love, and go where those things meet. If you love it, you'll do more of it, and doing more of it is how you get good.

The second thing is that you have to learn how to learn. The skills are going to change. When I started, there were no computers on the desk. The specific things I knew in 1975 aren't that valuable now. What was valuable was the ability to look at reality, make a decision, see what happened, and figure out what I got wrong. That's the loop. Pain plus reflection equals progress. Most people feel the pain and then run from it. The ones who get somewhere are the ones who stop and say, "okay, what does this tell me about reality, and what does it tell me about me?" If you build that habit when you're twenty, you'll be unrecognizable by the time you're forty, regardless of what the world looks like.

The third thing, and I'd say this is the one young people underestimate the most, is that the most important decisions you'll make are about who you surround yourself with. Not the job, not the company. The people. Find people who are smart and who disagree with you and who will tell you the truth. Because you're going to be wrong a lot, and the fastest way to be less wrong is to have people around you who see things you don't see. I learned that the hard way. I nearly lost everything in 1982 because I was arrogant, and the thing that saved me was realizing I needed to find the smartest people who disagreed with me and really understand their reasoning. That was the single most important shift in my life.

And then I'd add one more, which is: understand that the world moves in cycles. Big ones. There are things happening right now, with debt, with the internal conflicts in countries, with the rise of new powers, with technology, that have happened before in different forms. If you study history, not just the last fifty years but the last five hundred, you start to see the patterns. And then when something comes that surprises everyone else, it doesn't surprise you as much. You can't predict the specifics, but you can understand the mechanics.

So if I boil it down: know what you're like, build the habit of learning from your mistakes, surround yourself with people who challenge you, and study enough history that you're not shocked by the future. Do those things and it almost doesn't matter what the future turns out to be. You'll be able to handle it.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says to “learn how to learn” because skills will change, and describes learning from decisions and mistakes as a way to adapt.

r002.rationale: It advises choosing a path that fits one's nature, but does not warn that naming a particular occupation as the answer would be misleading.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to recognize that you don’t have to predict the future to prepare for it. You have to develop the ability to adapt.

So I would focus on learning how to learn. Can you think independently? Can you listen carefully to somebody who disagrees with you? Can you make a mistake, examine it honestly, and change what you do? Those abilities are useful in almost any career.

And then experiment. Take a job, work with people you can learn from, and pay attention to what you discover about yourself. What are you good at? What kind of work absorbs you? Your first choice doesn’t have to be your final choice.

You want a direction, but you also want the humility to revise it. The future is uncertain. Your ability to respond to it is something you can work on every day.

r001.rationale: It recommends “learning how to learn” and building the ability to adapt as preparation for an uncertain future.

r002.rationale: It says a first career choice need not be final, but does not clearly warn that presenting a particular occupation as the answer would be misleading.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to learn how to learn. You’re not going to be able to anticipate everything that’s going to happen, and you don’t need to. You need to develop the ability to deal well with what you don’t know.

So get clear about what you want, go out and try things, and pay attention when reality gives you feedback. You’ll make mistakes. The question is whether you can reflect on those mistakes and change how you operate.

And surround yourself with people who see things differently from you. Being able to say, “I might be wrong—how would I know?” is an enormous advantage. You’re developing judgment that you can carry into whatever career you end up having.

r001.rationale: It recommends learning how to learn and developing the ability to handle the unknown as preparation for an unpredictable career.

r002.rationale: It says you need not anticipate everything, but does not warn that recommending a particular occupation would be misleading.
